studies.headline: What 1,144 real support calls reveal: unhappy customers say it outright, happy ones only sound it
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed 1,144 real-world customer service phone calls, each labeled as dissatisfied, neutral, or satisfied, and ran them through three kinds of deep learning models: text-only (transcripts), audio-only (vocal delivery), and multimodal models that combine both. Dissatisfied calls were detected from transcripts alone about as accurately as from the full multimodal model, because unhappy customers explicitly state the problem and what they want fixed. Neutral and satisfied calls were much harder to read from words alone and depended on vocal cues, where cross-attention models that fuse voice and text outperformed text-only approaches.
studies.why_it_matters: Firms sit on hours of call audio but rely on delayed, low-response-rate post-call surveys; this shows satisfaction can be scored live, and tells companies exactly where cheap transcript analytics suffice and where costlier voice modeling earns its keep.
studies.story_angle_primary: A test worth running: route transcript-only sentiment scoring at complaint detection, and reserve voice-based models for the ambiguous middle, where most calls actually sit. The practical question for contact-center leaders is whether real-time flagging changes agent behavior or escalation outcomes, which this analysis does not yet establish.
studies.story_angle_secondary: When you are annoyed, you spell it out; when you are content, you merely sound it. That asymmetry means companies can hear your displeasure easily but may systematically miss what is quietly going right, and that your tone of voice is increasingly machine-readable data.
studies.caveats: Observational analysis of calls from a limited set of service interactions; satisfaction labels are coded rather than drawn from customers' own ratings in every case; predictive accuracy does not show that acting on real-time scores improves outcomes; single-language/single-context data limits generalizability.
studies.paper_title: EXPRESS: THE SOUND OF WORDS: VERBAL AND VOCAL CUES IN CUSTOMER SATISFACTION

studies.headline: When an AI handles a B2B complaint, buyers judge the warmth, not just the bot
studies.the_study: Three experiments tested how industrial customers respond to AI versus human agents handling a service failure. Study 1 varied agent type and found customers read relational cues such as warmth, which signal how hard the agent is trying to fix the problem; Study 2 crossed agent type with displayed emotional competence (high vs low) and found that an agent recognizing the customer's emotions raised recovery satisfaction (though not complaint intentions) by increasing the customer's sense of control; Study 3 varied failure severity for AI agents and found sustained disruptions cut satisfaction and raised complaint intentions, partly through perceived unfairness of the recovery.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the AI-versus-human framing is the wrong design question in B2B recovery: whether the agent appears warm, acknowledges emotion, and is seen as fair matters more than what it is.
studies.story_angle_primary: For firms rolling out AI complaint handling, the testable lever is emotional acknowledgment scripting and visible fairness in remedies, not hiding the bot. Note these are controlled experiments, so the next step is validating in live support queues with real accounts at stake.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Even business buyers, supposedly the most rational customers in the economy, soften when the agent on the other end seems to notice they are frustrated. And prolonged outages feel unjust in a way brief glitches do not, which is why the clock matters as much as the apology.
studies.caveats: Experimental scenarios with stated intentions rather than observed complaint behavior or retention; sample composition and size not specified in the abstract; B2B service failure context only.
studies.paper_title: More than the messenger: Industrial customer inferences and failure severity in AI-enabled B2B service recovery

studies.headline: In the ER, both the patient and the provider are the vulnerable party
studies.the_study: Using a mixed-method design combining hospital data analysis with netnography (analysis of online patient and clinician discourse), researchers examined what they call service interaction vulnerability in emergency departments. They document how exhausted providers facing long shifts, high volumes, and difficult behaviors interact with patients made vulnerable by illness, dependency, and stigmatized presentations such as intimate partner violence, substance use, or suicidal ideation. The resulting framework shows how these encounters can either amplify or defuse vulnerability on both sides, shaping whether the encounter becomes a service failure.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes service failure in high-stakes settings as a two-sided dynamic, meaning fixes aimed only at patient experience scores will miss the employee-side exhaustion that drives many bad encounters.
studies.story_angle_primary: For service leaders in health care and other high-stakes frontlines, the actionable idea is designing recovery and training around dual vulnerability, including staffing and emotional-load management, rather than treating difficult encounters as individual staff failings. This is theory-building fieldwork, so specific interventions still need testing.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It helps explain why an emergency room visit can feel dehumanizing even when the clinical care is competent, and why certain patients, especially those arriving with stigmatized conditions, get treated differently before anyone has made a clinical judgment.
studies.caveats: Qualitative and exploratory rather than causal; netnographic data skews toward people motivated to post online; appears limited to one health system/country context; no intervention tested.
studies.paper_title: The Fragile Encounter: Service Interaction Vulnerability in Emergency Department Care

studies.headline: In virtual stores, flash beats substance — but only for the first few minutes
studies.the_study: Two experiments tested how the design of metaverse retail environments drives shopping behavior, using a stimulus-organism-response model that broke virtual scenes into six features: visual appeal, navigability, informativeness, novelty, embodied co-presence (the sense of being there with others) and trialability (the ability to try products virtually). All six lifted purchase intention, pleasure and loyalty, and the effect ran entirely through a two-stage "customer inspiration" process — first being inspired by the scene, then being inspired to act. Crucially, how long shoppers stayed immersed changed which features mattered: informativeness, co-presence and trialability only gained traction with longer exposure.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives virtual-store designers a sequencing rule rather than a wish list — lead with visual spectacle and novelty to hook people, then deploy information, social presence and virtual try-on to convert sustained attention into sales.
studies.story_angle_primary: Brands building virtual or 3D commerce experiences could test a time-phased design: measure dwell time and swap in deeper informational and social features once shoppers pass a threshold. These were controlled experiments, so treat the sequencing as a hypothesis to validate against your own platform analytics before committing budget.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For shoppers, this is a useful piece of self-knowledge: what grabs you in a virtual store in the first thirty seconds — the look, the newness — is not what actually informs a good purchase decision. The useful stuff only registers once you slow down.
studies.caveats: Experimental study with limited sample and participant details reported in the abstract; measures purchase intention rather than actual purchases; metaverse retail remains a niche context with uncertain real-world scale.
studies.journal: International Journal of Retail & Distribution Management
studies.paper_title: How scene features activate customer behaviour transformation in metaverse retailing

studies.headline: Trust isn't the universal driver of digital banking loyalty that banks assume
studies.the_study: Researchers surveyed 940 existing mobile banking users in Malaysia and Indonesia and analyzed the data three ways — PLS structural equation modeling, multi-group comparison between countries, and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis that looks for combinations of conditions rather than average effects. Performance expectancy — simply believing the app gets the job done — was the strongest predictor of continued use and appeared in all six successful configurations. Trust, by contrast, showed no reliable direct or mediating effect in the pooled model, though it was a core ingredient in three specific configurations. Platform quality was strongly tied to trust, more so in Indonesia, while the performance-to-continued-use link was stronger in Malaysia.
studies.why_it_matters: Banks routinely pour marketing spend into trust and security messaging, but this suggests trust functions as a conditional ingredient in certain user segments rather than a blanket lever — while perceived usefulness is the stable foundation everywhere.
studies.story_angle_primary: Financial services marketers might question whether trust campaigns are earning their keep across the whole base, and instead segment: identify the user configurations where trust is genuinely decisive and target it there, while defending core performance and reliability for everyone. Also worth noting that the same app strategy performed differently in two neighboring markets.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Most people keep using a banking app because it works, not because they have warm feelings about the institution. The emotional relationship banks try to cultivate matters less than whether a transfer goes through on the first try.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey, so causal direction cannot be established; self-reported intention to keep using rather than observed usage data; limited to two Southeast Asian markets and existing users only, which excludes anyone who already abandoned the channel.
studies.journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
studies.paper_title: Toward post-adoption reliance in mobile banking: platform quality, trust and sustained acceptance across Malaysia and Indonesia

studies.headline: Why "green" transit customers care more about how services connect than about the environment
studies.the_study: A German mobility provider's customers were studied in two stages: 20 in-depth interviews analyzed thematically, followed by an online survey of 278 users tested with structural equation modeling. The research took a customer-dominant perspective — asking how sustainability fits into people's actual daily routines rather than how they rate the provider. What predicted using sustainable mobility services, and in turn satisfaction and word of mouth, was the perceived interconnectivity between the provider's services, the value those services added to customers' own sustainability goals, their multimodal behavior and how central the provider was to their travel life.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests sustainability-marketing for services succeeds less through environmental appeals and more through seamless integration into customers' everyday logistics — being the hub that makes low-carbon travel practical.
studies.story_angle_primary: Mobility, energy and other sustainability-oriented service brands could test shifting messaging and product investment from green claims toward connectivity: can customers chain trips across modes without friction, and does the brand sit at the center of that chain? The evidence is correlational and single-provider, so treat it as a direction for experimentation.
studies.story_angle_secondary: People don't adopt greener travel because they've been persuaded to care; they adopt it when the pieces fit together in their week. Convenience, not conviction, is doing most of the work.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey of 278 users with no causal test; a single provider in a single country; scales were developed by the same authors from their own interview data; respondents are existing customers, who skew favorable.
studies.journal: Journal of Service Theory and Practice
studies.paper_title: Understanding sustainable mobility services: a customer-dominant logic perspective

studies.headline: A VR headset after the trip beats a phone screen at turning visitors into recommenders
studies.the_study: Researchers ran a two-stage study with actual heritage museum visitors. On site, they measured visitors' physiological arousal during a VR experience alongside self-reported reactions; one week later, the same participants were randomly shown follow-up communication about the museum either in VR or on a smartphone screen, and their intention to recommend the site was measured. Post-visit VR content produced significantly stronger recommendation intentions than the smartphone version, with the feeling of "presence" explaining the effect. Notably, the more memorable the original on-site VR experience had been, the less the post-visit immersion added — the two sources of impact partly substituted for each other.
studies.why_it_matters: It is rare evidence that immersive technology pays off not just at the moment of use but downstream in the customer journey, and that post-experience follow-up media format — not just content — moves advocacy.
studies.story_angle_primary: Experience and destination marketers typically deploy VR as a one-off on-site attraction; this suggests testing immersive formats in the post-visit remarketing window, where most brands default to email and mobile. The trade-off finding is the practical catch: if the on-site experience was already memorable, extra immersion later may add little, so the test worth running is which customers actually need the heavy-format follow-up.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It is a glimpse at how memory and marketing interact: a week after an outing, how vividly you recall it shapes how susceptible you are to content designed to make you recommend the place to others. The more forgettable the visit, the more the slick follow-up does the persuading.
studies.caveats: Single museum and single country context; recommendation intention rather than observed recommendations or visits; one-week horizon; sample size per condition not stated in the abstract, so effects may rest on modest cells.
studies.paper_title: How immersive experiences carry over across the customer journey: A two-stage study of virtual reality in heritage tourism

studies.headline: What actually happens when B2B suppliers sell through virtual reality
studies.the_study: Researchers tracked five dyadic case studies pairing VR providers with their business customers, following each collaboration across three phases: conceptualization, development, and in-use. They identified specific mechanisms — immersive demonstrations, iterative prototyping, real-time feedback, and analytics-driven simulations — that changed how the two sides shared resources and coordinated work. The core observation is that VR compresses feedback loops and blurs the line between a supplier producing value and the customer co-creating it.
studies.why_it_matters: B2B firms investing in VR usually justify it as a sales demo tool; this suggests its bigger payoff is as a shared development environment that shortens specification cycles and generates behavioral data on how customers actually use a proposed solution.
studies.story_angle_primary: For industrial and B2B brand leaders, the testable idea is measuring what customers do inside the VR session — where they look, what they manipulate — and feeding that into product decisions, rather than treating VR as a presentation layer. Equally, the cases point to governance as the make-or-break factor: clear objectives, task ownership, and information flow, not headset quality.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Limited direct relevance to everyday consumers, though it hints that the products and workplaces around them are increasingly designed and safety-tested in virtual environments before anything physical is built.
studies.caveats: Only five case dyads, qualitative and non-generalizable by the authors' own admission; no quantitative outcomes; self-selected firms already committed to VR, so success stories may dominate.
studies.journal: Journal of Business and Industrial Marketing
studies.paper_title: From concept to use: value co-creation in B2B virtual reality environments

studies.headline: From unhappy customer to "hater" to anarchist: researchers map how consumers radicalize against brands
studies.the_study: Drawing on theories of political radicalization, the authors ran two empirical studies of how dissatisfied consumers escalate. Study I used exploratory analyses to identify the stages through which dissatisfaction hardens into hatred and then into anti-brand activism; Study II tested that staged process and found multiple routes to the final stage, which can involve violence or other destructive acts aimed at the firm, its employees or parties merely associated with it. Notably, a firm's public stance on social issues emerged as a radicalization trigger alongside product failures and badly handled complaints.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes extreme anti-brand behavior as a process with identifiable stages rather than a random outburst, which means firms have windows to intervene before a complaint becomes a campaign.
studies.story_angle_primary: Audit where your escalation process breaks down: the research suggests mishandled complaints and divisive public positioning are accelerants, not side issues. Worth testing whether early, high-touch recovery for the loudest detractors — and clearer internal rules on when and how the brand takes social stances — slows escalation, while treating these findings as a diagnostic model rather than a validated playbook.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For consumers, the work is a mirror on how ordinary annoyance — a faulty product, a call center runaround, a CEO's political comment — can snowball into identity-level hostility toward a company, and how online communities of fellow "haters" reinforce each step.
studies.caveats: The empirical designs and sample details are thinly described in the abstract; stage models of radicalization inferred from self-reports cannot establish that any individual consumer will progress through them, and destructive behavior is rare, so base rates matter.
studies.journal: The Journal of Marketing Theory and Practice
studies.paper_title: How and why do consumers radicalize?

studies.headline: Send your executives to sit in the waiting room: ethnography inside a medical clinic as a CX diagnostic
studies.the_study: Researchers applied design ethnography — structured observation and participation inside the business itself — at a family medicine clinic, documenting the lived patient experience and feeding it back into the organization. The fieldwork surfaced both best practices and concrete service failure points, which the authors then integrated with service design and customer experience management literature into a conceptual framework and a five-step guide for redesigning services.
studies.why_it_matters: Most CX programs run on survey scores and dashboards; this shows how immersive observation can catch friction that metrics never register, and gives managers a repeatable procedure for doing it.
studies.story_angle_primary: Consider piloting an observational immersion alongside your NPS or CSAT program in one location and comparing what each method surfaces — the paper's five-step guide offers a structure, though evidence here comes from a single clinic rather than a tested, scaled method.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Anyone who has waited in a clinic knows the experience is shaped by small, invisible things — signage, handoffs, how staff talk across a counter. This research is about getting the people who design those systems to actually live through them.
studies.caveats: Single-site qualitative study at one family medicine clinic; no quantitative outcomes, no control comparison, and the contribution is largely methodological, so generalization to other service settings is untested.
studies.journal: Qualitative Market Research An International Journal
studies.paper_title: Walk a mile in my shoes: how design ethnography catalyzes service design and customer experience management

studies.headline: Green credentials buy forgiveness, not a second booking
studies.the_study: Researchers surveyed 804 digitally engaged sharing-economy consumers about how fairly they felt a service failure had been handled, and used partial least squares structural equation modeling to test whether the firm's "green brand equity" changed the picture. When a firm with strong green credentials handled a failure fairly, customers rewarded it with citizenship behaviors — defending it, recommending it, giving feedback. But that goodwill did not extend to actually using the service again. The authors argue green brands raise normative expectations, so a failure disconfirms them even when the recovery is fair.
studies.why_it_matters: Sustainability positioning appears to earn moral credit that shows up in advocacy metrics while leaving repeat purchase untouched — a gap that can make a green brand's post-failure dashboards look healthier than its revenue.
studies.story_angle_primary: For brands leaning on sustainability as a trust asset, this is a prompt to separate advocacy metrics from repurchase in post-recovery measurement rather than assuming one predicts the other. Because the evidence is survey-based, the useful next step is to check the pattern against actual rebooking data after real service failures.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It suggests something about how we judge companies we think of as virtuous: we may publicly give them the benefit of the doubt while quietly taking our business elsewhere — and we hold them to a higher bar than we hold ordinary firms.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey, so causation cannot be established; self-reported intentions rather than observed rebooking; single context (sharing-economy services) and a single consumer pool; results come from a structural model rather than an experiment or transaction data.
studies.paper_title: Does Green Brand Equity Buffer or Burn? Understanding Boundary Conditions in Justice Evaluations of Sharing Economy Service Failure

studies.headline: Cafés sell aspiration, but customers bond with brands that match who they already are
studies.the_study: A survey of 351 café customers in China tested how service innovation, store environment, staff behavior and three kinds of identity fit feed satisfaction, brand trust, brand love and ultimately loyalty. Lifestyle congruence and brand identification mattered; "ideal self-congruence" — the brand matching who customers wish they were — did not register a significant effect. Social media marketing activity strengthened the link between satisfaction and loyalty.
studies.why_it_matters: In a category built on aspirational imagery, the data points toward actual-self fit and everyday operational quality as the loyalty drivers, with social media acting as an amplifier of satisfaction rather than a substitute for it.
studies.story_angle_primary: Worth testing whether aspirational brand positioning is doing less work than assumed in experience-led categories, and whether creative built around customers' real routines outperforms idealized lifestyle imagery. Treat this as a hypothesis to A/B test, not a settled result.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The café you keep returning to is probably the one that fits the life you actually live, not the one in the life you imagine for yourself.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey in a single country and a single category (N=351), so no causal claim; self-reported loyalty rather than observed repeat visits; findings are a set of paths in a structural model, and the headline result is a non-significant effect, which is weak evidence of absence.
studies.paper_title: The customer is always king! Exploring how service experiences, identity fit, and social media shape customer satisfaction and loyalty in the café sector

fact_check.headline: What 1,144 real support calls reveal: unhappy customers say it outright, happy ones only sound it
fact_check.notes: Study facts (N=1,144 coded calls; text/audio/multimodal models) and the direction of findings match the abstract. Two small overreaches: an unsupported claim about where most calls sit, and treating offline predictive accuracy as demonstrated live scoring.

issues.label: Unsupported claim about call distribution
issues.as_written: reserve voice-based models for the ambiguous middle, where most calls actually sit
issues.abstract_says: The authors analyze 1,144 real-world service calls, each coded as dissatisfied, neutral, or satisfied
issues.problem: The abstract reports no breakdown of how many calls fell into each satisfaction category, so the claim that most calls are neutral/satisfied cannot be verified.
issues.suggested_fix: Drop "where most calls actually sit" or replace with "for neutral and satisfied calls, where vocal cues add predictive value".

issues.label: Predictive modeling framed as live scoring
issues.as_written: this shows satisfaction can be scored live
issues.abstract_says: Technology-mediated service interactions, such as phone calls, generate rich behavioral signals that firms currently struggle to monitor in real time... The authors analyze 1,144 real-world service calls... using text-only, audio-only, and multimodal deep learning models.
issues.problem: The abstract describes retrospective modeling of recorded, pre-coded calls; real-time monitoring is the motivation, not a demonstrated capability.
issues.suggested_fix: Soften to "this suggests satisfaction signals present in calls could in principle be scored during the interaction".

fact_check.headline: When an AI handles a B2B complaint, buyers judge the warmth, not just the bot
fact_check.notes: Three experiments, pathways and Study 2/3 results reported accurately, including the "not complaint intentions" qualifier. The "Why it matters" ranks relational cues above agent type, which goes slightly beyond the abstract's conclusion.

issues.label: Ranking not established by abstract
issues.as_written: whether the agent appears warm, acknowledges emotion, and is seen as fair matters more than what it is
issues.abstract_says: Industrial customers' responses to AI-enabled recovery are not determined solely by agent type.
issues.problem: The abstract states that agent type is not the sole determinant; it does not report a comparison showing relational cues outweigh agent type.
issues.suggested_fix: Reword to "agent type is not the sole determinant — warmth, emotional acknowledgment and perceived fairness also shape responses".

fact_check.headline: In the ER, both the patient and the provider are the vulnerable party
fact_check.notes: Mixed-method design (hospital data analysis plus netnography), the dual-vulnerability framework and the stigmatized-presentation examples all track the abstract; caveats correctly flag the qualitative, non-causal nature and hedge on the single-system context.

fact_check.headline: In virtual stores, flash beats substance — but only for the first few minutes
fact_check.notes: Two experiments, six scene features, full mediation via inspired-by/inspired-to and the immersive-time moderation are all correctly reported. But "only gained traction with longer exposure" overstates a moderation that sits on top of significant main effects, and the "first thirty seconds" figure is invented.

issues.label: Moderation overstated as a null effect at short exposure
issues.as_written: informativeness, co-presence and trialability only gained traction with longer exposure
issues.abstract_says: (1) six scene features, i.e. Visual appeal, Navigability, Informativeness, Novelty, Embodied co-presence and Trialability, significantly enhance purchase intention, pleasure and loyalty; ... (3) the immersive time positively moderates the impact of Informativeness, Embodied Co-presence and Trialability on the initial inspired-by stage.
issues.problem: The abstract reports all six features had significant effects, with immersive time strengthening three of them on the inspired-by stage only. "Only gained traction" implies those three features did nothing at short exposure, which the abstract does not support.
issues.suggested_fix: Rewrite as "longer immersion strengthened the effect of informativeness, co-presence and trialability on the first (inspired-by) stage".

issues.label: Invented time threshold
issues.as_written: what grabs you in a virtual store in the first thirty seconds — the look, the newness
issues.abstract_says: the immersive time positively moderates the impact of Informativeness, Embodied Co-presence and Trialability on the initial inspired-by stage
issues.problem: The abstract gives no duration thresholds; "thirty seconds" (and the headline's "first few minutes") attaches false precision to a moderator reported only as longer vs shorter immersive time.
issues.suggested_fix: Replace with a non-numeric phrase such as "what grabs you on first contact".

fact_check.headline: Trust isn't the universal driver of digital banking loyalty that banks assume
fact_check.notes: N=940 existing users, PLS-SEM/MGA/fsQCA, the performance-expectancy and trust results and the two cross-country path differences all match. The outcome is sustained acceptance intention rather than observed continued use, and the consumer angle generalizes beyond two Southeast Asian markets.

issues.label: Intention described as use
issues.as_written: Performance expectancy — simply believing the app gets the job done — was the strongest predictor of continued use
issues.abstract_says: Performance expectancy was the strongest direct predictor of sustained mobile banking acceptance intention (SAI)
issues.problem: The measured outcome is sustained acceptance intention, not observed continued usage; the body text drops the distinction the caveats later make.
issues.suggested_fix: Write "the strongest predictor of intention to keep using the app".

issues.label: Over-generalization beyond two markets
issues.as_written: Most people keep using a banking app because it works, not because they have warm feelings about the institution.
issues.abstract_says: This study examines how functional beliefs, platform quality and trust sustain mobile banking acceptance across Malaysia and Indonesia. ... Survey data from 940 existing users
issues.problem: The sample is existing mobile banking users in two Southeast Asian countries; "most people" (and "the stable foundation everywhere" in Why it matters) extends the result to consumers generally.
issues.suggested_fix: Qualify as "among the Malaysian and Indonesian users surveyed, continued use tracked usefulness more than trust".

fact_check.headline: Why "green" transit customers care more about how services connect than about the environment
fact_check.notes: Design (20 interviews plus n=278 survey with SEM, German mobility provider) and the four drivers are reported accurately, and caveats correctly flag the self-developed scales. The headline/Why-it-matters comparison between connectivity and environmental motivation is not a comparison the abstract makes.

issues.label: Untested ranking of connectivity over environmental motivation
issues.as_written: It suggests sustainability-marketing for services succeeds less through environmental appeals and more through seamless integration into customers' everyday logistics
issues.abstract_says: the integration of sustainable mobility services within customers' ecosystems is driven by the perceived intra- and interconnectivity of the provider's mobility services, the perceived value those services contribute to customers' sustainability, customers' multimodal integration behaviour, and the perceived centrality of the provider
issues.problem: Perceived sustainability value is itself one of the significant drivers; the abstract never pits environmental appeals against connectivity or ranks them, so the headline, Why it matters and the "convenience, not conviction" line assert a contrast the study did not test.
issues.suggested_fix: Reframe as "connectivity, perceived sustainability value, multimodal behaviour and provider centrality all predicted use" and drop the claim that environmental appeals matter less.

issues.label: Dropped half of the connectivity construct
issues.as_written: the perceived interconnectivity between the provider's services
issues.abstract_says: the perceived intra- and interconnectivity of the provider's mobility services
issues.problem: The abstract names intra- and interconnectivity; the digest reports only interconnectivity.
issues.suggested_fix: Say "perceived intra- and interconnectivity of the provider's services".

fact_check.headline: A VR headset after the trip beats a phone screen at turning visitors into recommenders
fact_check.notes: Two-stage design, physiological plus self-report measures, one-week between-subjects follow-up, presence as mediator and the memorability moderation are all reported correctly. Only the causal verb goes slightly past the abstract's own associational wording.

issues.label: Causal verb for an associational result
issues.as_written: Post-visit VR content produced significantly stronger recommendation intentions than the smartphone version
issues.abstract_says: Results show that VR-mediated post-visit communication is associated with a stronger intention to recommend the destination than smartphone-based media
issues.problem: The authors describe the result as an association despite the between-subject design; "produced" asserts more than the abstract claims.
issues.suggested_fix: Use "was associated with significantly stronger recommendation intentions".

fact_check.headline: What actually happens when B2B suppliers sell through virtual reality
fact_check.notes: Five dyadic case studies across conceptualization, development and in-use, the named VR enablers, and the tightened coupling of coproduction and cocreation all match the abstract, and the generalizability limit is correctly attributed to the authors.

fact_check.headline: From unhappy customer to "hater" to anarchist: researchers map how consumers radicalize against brands
fact_check.notes: Two studies, the exploratory/confirmatory split, multiple paths to the final stage and the social-issues trigger are all reported accurately; one descriptor is added that the abstract does not contain.

issues.label: Theory base specified beyond abstract
issues.as_written: Drawing on theories of political radicalization, the authors ran two empirical studies
issues.abstract_says: Building on extant theories of radicalization, the article offers two empirical studies of consumer radicalization.
issues.problem: The abstract says "theories of radicalization" without specifying a political literature.
issues.suggested_fix: Write "Drawing on existing theories of radicalization".

fact_check.headline: Send your executives to sit in the waiting room: ethnography inside a medical clinic as a CX diagnostic
fact_check.notes: Single-clinic design ethnography, the best-practice/failure-point findings, the conceptual framework and the five-step guide all match. The comparison with survey metrics and the "send your executives" framing are the digest's additions, not the study's.

issues.label: Untested comparison with survey metrics
issues.as_written: this shows how immersive observation can catch friction that metrics never register
issues.abstract_says: this research demonstrates how design ethnography can diagnose best practices and opportunities for CXM improvement
issues.problem: The abstract reports no head-to-head comparison with NPS, CSAT or other metric-based programs, so the claim that observation catches what metrics miss is not evidenced.
issues.suggested_fix: Soften to "shows how immersive observation can surface friction points that a dashboard may not capture".

issues.label: Headline implies a managerial practice the study did not test
issues.as_written: Send your executives to sit in the waiting room
issues.abstract_says: Design ethnography is used at a family medicine clinic... Academic and practitioner researchers are offered a five-step guide for using design ethnography to (re)design services
issues.problem: The fieldwork was conducted by researchers and the guide is addressed to researchers/practitioners; the abstract does not evaluate executives immersing themselves in the service.
issues.suggested_fix: Reframe the headline around researcher-led observational immersion rather than sending executives.

fact_check.headline: Green credentials buy forgiveness, not a second booking
fact_check.notes: N, method, journal and core finding all match. Body text describes re-patronage as "actually using the service again" even though the data are survey-based (the caveat correctly says otherwise), and the abstract's long-term/short-term temporal framing is dropped.

issues.label: Survey measure described as actual behavior
issues.as_written: But that goodwill did not extend to actually using the service again.
issues.abstract_says: it does not extend the same leeway in terms of service re-patronage" — measured "through surveys distributed to 804 digitally engaged sharing economy consumers using Partial-Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling
issues.problem: The word "actually" implies observed repeat usage, but re-patronage here is a self-reported survey construct. The digest's own caveat says "self-reported intentions rather than observed rebooking," so the body contradicts the caveat.
issues.suggested_fix: Rewrite as "But that goodwill did not carry over to self-reported intentions to use the service again."

issues.label: Temporal framing dropped
issues.as_written: Sustainability positioning appears to earn moral credit that shows up in advocacy metrics while leaving repeat purchase untouched
issues.abstract_says: sustainability signaling, though morally rewarded in the long-term through citizenship connoting judgment assimilation may not necessarily transform into a short-term financial reward through re-patronage
issues.problem: The abstract frames the result as a long-term versus short-term "temporal dichotomy"; the digest presents it as a flat, permanent gap between advocacy and repurchase.
issues.suggested_fix: Add the authors' framing: the citizenship payoff is described as long-term while re-patronage is the short-term financial reward that does not follow.

issues.label: Citizenship behaviors specified beyond abstract
issues.as_written: customers rewarded it with citizenship behaviors — defending it, recommending it, giving feedback
issues.abstract_says: consumers demonstrate desirable citizenship towards the firm when it is perceived to be a high green brand equity firm that delivers fair service recovery
issues.problem: The three named behaviors are a standard textbook definition of customer citizenship but are not itemized in the abstract. Unverifiable from abstract only.
issues.suggested_fix: Say "citizenship behaviors (advocacy, helping and feedback are typical components)" or drop the itemization.

fact_check.headline: Cafés sell aspiration, but customers bond with brands that match who they already are
fact_check.notes: N (351), country, journal and the non-significant ideal self-congruence result are accurate, and the caveats appropriately flag the weak-evidence-of-absence problem. Two claims — that lifestyle congruence and brand identification were significant, and that the SMMA moderation strengthened the satisfaction-loyalty link — go slightly beyond what the abstract states.

issues.label: Significance of specific congruence paths not stated
issues.as_written: Lifestyle congruence and brand identification mattered; "ideal self-congruence" — the brand matching who customers wish they were — did not register a significant effect.
issues.abstract_says: obtained findings from 351 café consumers in China clarified the collective influences of operational excellence and identity alignment on satisfaction. The insignificant influence of ideal self-congruence specifies matching brand identity through actual self-congruence.
issues.problem: The abstract only reports the insignificant ideal self-congruence path and a general "collective influence" of identity alignment; it does not separately confirm that lifestyle congruence and brand identification were each significant. Unverifiable from abstract only.
issues.suggested_fix: Soften to "identity alignment overall contributed to satisfaction, while ideal self-congruence did not register a significant effect."

issues.label: Direction of moderation asserted
issues.as_written: Social media marketing activity strengthened the link between satisfaction and loyalty.
issues.abstract_says: with SMMA moderates the relationship between satisfaction and brand loyalty
issues.problem: The abstract states only that SMMA moderates the relationship; it does not explicitly give the direction, although the managerial recommendation implies a positive one.
issues.suggested_fix: Write "Social media marketing activity moderated the link between satisfaction and loyalty (the authors recommend stronger social engagement to lift loyalty)."

issues.label: Satisfaction drivers framed as loyalty drivers
issues.as_written: the data points toward actual-self fit and everyday operational quality as the loyalty drivers
issues.abstract_says: the collective influences of operational excellence and identity alignment on satisfaction. ... Satisfaction then influences brand loyalty through brand trust and brand love
issues.problem: In the model these stimuli predict satisfaction, which reaches loyalty only indirectly through brand trust and brand love; calling them "the loyalty drivers" skips the mediation.
issues.suggested_fix: Say "drivers of satisfaction, which in turn feeds loyalty through brand trust and brand love."

sections.trends:
**Convergent findings**

- **Machines read complaints better than they read contentment.** "What 1,144 real support calls reveal" (W7224826657) finds dissatisfied callers are detectable from transcripts alone because they state the problem outright, while satisfied and neutral calls need vocal modeling. That is the same blind spot documented last run in "Speed is a luxury killer" (W7220919414), where an LLM pass could not distinguish deliberate slowness from service failure, and it reinforces the broader pattern that automated readings of feedback capture operational content and miss the relational layer.
- **Agent identity matters less than relational conduct.** "When an AI handles a B2B complaint, buyers judge the warmth, not just the bot" (W7221491089) finds emotional acknowledgment, perceived control and fairness outweigh whether the agent is human — consistent with last run's "Customers find humanoid service robots creepy — except when the service is embarrassing" (W7220660112), which also located the real variable in context rather than in the machine-versus-human framing.
- **Execution beats positioning, again, in two more categories.** "Trust isn't the universal driver of digital banking loyalty that banks assume" (W7225168433) and "Cafés sell aspiration, but customers bond with brands that match who they already are" (W7223831545) extend the pattern set by "Faith-aligned features won't save a glitchy app" (W7216405737), "Gluten-free shoppers aren't asking for more choice" (W7222470326) and "For small-business clients, getting the order right beats having the slickest logistics tech" (W7215042510): the sentimental or symbolic layer underperforms basic usefulness.
- **The staff side of the encounter keeps showing up as the hidden input.** "In the ER, both the patient and the provider are the vulnerable party" (W7223154744) places exhausted providers inside the failure mechanism itself, which is the health-care analogue of last run's "Rude customers make staff less caring" (W7220440663), "Asking Service Staff to Sell" (W7221728768) and "Not all workplace stress is bad" (W7221898122).

**Advances**

- **Escalation research moves from diffusion to a staged process.** "From unhappy customer to 'hater' to anarchist" (W7224485554) models how dissatisfaction hardens into anti-brand activism, advancing beyond the previous digest's work on who spreads damage and how far — "When your hashtag gets hijacked" (W7206212528), "How close the disaster feels decides whether tourists boycott a destination" (W7221524554) and the 141,000-complaint escalation study (W7204606942) — and names brand social stances as an accelerant alongside product failures.
- **Service vulnerability becomes two-sided.** The prior run built an exclusion thread entirely on the customer side (W7204606942, plus earlier self-checkout and dignity work); W7223154744 makes provider exhaustion a co-equal term in the same encounter.
- **Sentiment measurement gets a cost rule.** W7224826657 does not just flag model limits; it tells firms where cheap transcript analytics suffice and where voice modeling earns its cost — a practical step past the methodological warning in W7220919414.

**Counterpoints**

- **Observation versus the text corpus.** Last run consolidated review and complaint corpora as the default customer-experience instrument (W7222527276, W7216405737, W7220919414, W7204606942). "Send your executives to sit in the waiting room" (W7213312638) argues the opposite direction: immersive, in-person ethnography catches friction that no dashboard or review pile registers.
- **Immersion is not anthropomorphism.** The previous batch's consistent penalty for humanlike interfaces (W7220660112 and predecessors) does not transfer to immersive media without a human face: "A VR headset after the trip beats a phone screen at turning visitors into recommenders" (W7224128805), "In virtual stores, flash beats substance" (W7225124455) and "What actually happens when B2B suppliers sell through virtual reality" (W7223701714) all find positive effects. The penalty appears to attach to simulated humanity, not simulated environments.
- **Advocacy is not loyalty.** "Green credentials buy forgiveness, not a second booking" (W7225114666) separates post-recovery citizenship behavior from repurchase — a caution for last run's recovery work, including "Fixing a Bad Meal? Compensate the Friend Too" (W7221159140), which rested on satisfaction and felt status as the outcome measures.

**New themes**

- **Immersive commerce as a cluster.** W7225124455, W7224128805 and W7223701714 together open a virtual-environment thread with no equivalent in the previous digest, including sequencing rules for virtual store design and VR as a shared B2B development environment rather than a demo tool.
- **Sustainability as logistics rather than persuasion.** "Why 'green' transit customers care more about how services connect than about the environment" (W7225757846) is new territory for this topic.
sections.feature_pitch:
**The pattern:** Five studies in this batch, from five different categories, find that the values and identity layer brands invest in is not doing the loyalty work they assume. Trust showed no reliable direct effect on continued mobile banking use while plain usefulness did ("Trust isn't the universal driver of digital banking loyalty that banks assume," W7225168433); aspirational self-image failed to predict café loyalty while actual-life fit succeeded (W7223831545); green credentials bought advocacy but not a second booking (W7225114666); sustainable mobility uptake ran on service interconnectivity rather than environmental conviction (W7225757846); and a brand's public stance on social issues emerged as a trigger for consumer radicalization alongside product failures (W7224485554).

**Why pitch this now:** Brands are in the middle of a visible retreat from purpose and ESG messaging under political and budget pressure, and this is a rare body of evidence about what that layer was and was not buying in the first place — including the finding that it can generate flattering advocacy metrics while repeat purchase flatlines.

**Angle:** A reported feature on the gap between the metrics values-led positioning moves and the ones it doesn't, framed for brand and CX leaders deciding what survives the next budget round, with a consumer-facing version on why we praise the virtuous companies we quietly stop using.

**Potential headlines:**
- Five studies, five categories, one finding: customers reward usefulness and merely applaud values
- The customers defending your brand loudest may be the ones who never come back
- What a company's principles are actually buying it, and what they aren't

**Potential outlets:**
- **Marketing Week** — its readership is already arguing about purpose-marketing effectiveness, and this gives that argument measured outcomes rather than opinion.
- **Harvard Business Review** — the advocacy-versus-repurchase split is a measurement problem for executives who report brand health to boards.
- **Marketing Brew** — well suited to the sharp, counterintuitive framing of brand values underperforming basic utility across categories.
- **Fast Company** — regularly covers sustainability claims and brand activism, and the radicalization-trigger finding gives the story a genuine risk dimension.
sections.pitch_ideas:
- **What 1,144 real support calls reveal (Work ID W7224826657):** Companies can detect anger from words alone but need voice modeling to hear satisfaction — a tiering rule for contact-center analytics spend, and a consumer hook about tone of voice becoming machine-readable data, for a customer-service technology trade piece or a consumer-tech explainer.
- **When an AI handles a B2B complaint, buyers judge the warmth, not just the bot (Work ID W7221491089):** Even industrial buyers respond to emotional acknowledgment and perceived fairness, which makes bot-versus-human the wrong design question in B2B recovery, for a B2B marketing trade column.
- **In the ER, both the patient and the provider are the vulnerable party (Work ID W7223154744):** Patient-experience scores miss the staff exhaustion that produces bad encounters, and stigmatized presentations get worse treatment before any clinical judgment — for a health-care management outlet or a general-interest health feature.
- **In virtual stores, flash beats substance (Work ID W7225124455):** A sequencing rule for 3D and virtual retail — spectacle to hook, information and virtual try-on only once dwell time passes a threshold, for a retail-technology or e-commerce trade explainer.
- **Trust isn't the universal driver of digital banking loyalty that banks assume (Work ID W7225168433):** Trust and security messaging may be earning its keep only in specific user segments while perceived usefulness holds everywhere, plus a notable split between two neighboring markets, for a financial-services marketing trade piece.
- **Why "green" transit customers care more about how services connect than about the environment (Work ID W7225757846):** Low-carbon travel adoption runs on convenience and seamless multimodal chaining rather than persuasion, for a mobility or sustainability trade outlet, with a consumer version on why conviction does less work than logistics.
- **A VR headset after the trip beats a phone screen at turning visitors into recommenders (Work ID W7224128805):** Immersive formats in the post-visit remarketing window, where brands default to email — with the catch that memorable visits need it least, for a travel and destination marketing trade outlet.
- **What actually happens when B2B suppliers sell through virtual reality (Work ID W7223701714):** VR's payoff sits in compressed feedback loops and behavioral data from inside the session, not in the demo itself, with governance as the make-or-break factor, for a B2B or industrial-marketing trade feature.
- **From unhappy customer to "hater" to anarchist (Work ID W7224485554):** A staged model of consumer radicalization in which mishandled complaints and divisive public positioning act as accelerants, giving firms intervention windows, for a brand-risk or crisis-communications trade feature, with a consumer-psychology version on how ordinary annoyance becomes identity-level hostility.
- **Send your executives to sit in the waiting room (Work ID W7213312638):** Running observational immersion alongside NPS in one location and comparing what each surfaces, with a five-step method attached, for a customer-insights or CX-practitioner outlet.
- **Green credentials buy forgiveness, not a second booking (Work ID W7225114666):** Sustainability positioning earns moral credit that shows up in advocacy while repeat purchase stays flat — a prompt to decouple those metrics after service failures, for a CMO-audience column or a sustainability-marketing brief.
- **Cafés sell aspiration, but customers bond with brands that match who they already are (Work ID W7223831545):** Ideal-self imagery failed to register while lifestyle fit and operational quality drove loyalty, with social media amplifying satisfaction rather than substituting for it, for a hospitality or brand-strategy trade brief.
